analysis.one_liner: Lets health insurers pick whichever state's rules govern their plans and repeals core Affordable Care Act coverage protections.
analysis.headline: Referred to three House committees and its subcommittees in February 2013, the bill never received a vote before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would do two things. It would wipe out title I of the Affordable Care Act — the part of the law that set nationwide rules for health insurance, such as protecting people with pre-existing conditions and expanding coverage. It would also let each insurance company choose one "home state" whose insurance laws would govern the plans it sells in every other state, freeing the company from the rules of the states where its customers actually live. The bill never advanced past committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: If it passed, health insurers would gain the right to pick their own regulator and sell plans nationwide under the lightest rules available, avoiding state coverage mandates and consumer protections. Healthy individuals who could buy cheaper, skinnier plans would also come out ahead in the short run.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Health insurers; healthy buyers seeking cheaper plans

how_it_helps.text: Repeals title I of the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act and related provisions of the Health Care and Education Reconciliation Act of 2010, and restores the prior law that those provisions replaced.

Lets each insurance issuer designate one "primary state" whose covered laws govern its individual health plans in every state, and exempts the issuer from any secondary state's laws that would prohibit or regulate its operation there.

Requires plans sold into another state to carry a notice stating the policy may be less expensive because it is not subject to all of that state's insurance laws, mandated benefits, consumer protection laws, or restrictions on rate changes.

Includes some narrower safeguards for people who buy the new out-of-state plans: limits on reclassifying or raising premiums based on health status at renewal, an independent external appeal process for denied claims, a requirement that the primary state use a risk-based capital formula, and a disclosure notice in bold 12-point type.

analysis.who_pays: People with pre-existing conditions and other sicker or older consumers would lose the most: repealing ACA title I would restore medical underwriting, and cheaper bare-bones out-of-state plans would pull healthier people out of risk pools, raising costs for everyone left. State insurance regulators would also lose authority over plans sold to their own residents.
analysis.who_pays_short: People with pre-existing conditions; state insurance regulators

drawbacks.text: Repealing ACA title I would erase the law's coverage expansion requirements and protections for the individual insurance market, including the rules protecting people with pre-existing conditions, and restore the pre-2010 legal landscape.

Insurers selling into a state would be exempt from that state's laws regulating their operation, and the primary state would have sole jurisdiction to enforce its own insurance laws in every secondary state, leaving a resident's own state regulator largely powerless over the plan they bought.

The bill's own required notice tells buyers their policy may be cheaper precisely because it is not subject to the secondary state's mandated benefits, consumer protection laws, or restrictions on rate changes.

The bill orders a Government Accountability Office study of its effects on the number of uninsured and underinsured people, the availability and cost of coverage for people with pre-existing conditions, and the elimination or reduction of benefits — an acknowledgment that these were the open questions the bill's backers could not answer.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Supporters could honestly argue that letting people buy cheaper plans would lower premiums for some healthy buyers, and the bill does attach a disclosure notice, external appeals, and a premium-increase limit to the new out-of-state plans. But the centerpiece is repealing ACA title I, which would trade strong, universal market protections for a patchwork in which each insurer picks its own rules. The people most likely to be hurt — those with pre-existing conditions and other expensive health needs — are exactly the people the old pre-ACA rules failed. The bill does not seriously address that trade-off beyond requiring a study of it after the fact.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees and two of their subcommittees in early 2013 and never moved again; the Congress ended without any committee or floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Marsha Blackburn introduced the bill on February 15, 2013 with fifteen original cosponsors, all Republicans.
The same day, the House referred it to the Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Education and the Workforce Committees.
It was then referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health and, in April 2013, to the Education and the Workforce Subcommittee on Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions.
No further action was ever recorded; the bill never reached a committee vote or the House floor before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumers who rely on the ACA's individual-market protections — especially people with pre-existing conditions — are better off because the bill never advanced, and state insurance regulators kept full authority over plans sold to their residents. Health insurers did not get the interstate framework that would have let them choose their own regulator.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: People relying on ACA coverage protections

sides.party_line_note: All 24 supporters on record — the sponsor and 23 cosponsors — were Republicans, and because the bill never reached a vote, no recorded opposition ever materialized.

industries.note: The bill would let each insurer designate a primary state whose rules govern plans sold nationwide, freeing insurers from other states' coverage mandates, consumer protections, and rate-change restrictions. The gain for insurers comes from shedding rules that protect consumers, and the bill's own disclosure notice warns buyers their policy may skip mandated benefits and rate protections — costs that would fall hardest on sicker policyholders.

States would lose most authority to regulate or block individual plans sold to their own residents when the issuer designates another state as its primary state, keeping only narrow powers such as financial examinations, fraud enforcement, and unfair-claims-practice rules. State regulators have historically opposed letting insurers shop for the friendliest regulator.

Repealing ACA title I and allowing underwriting based on health status would remove the protections that make coverage affordable for people with expensive medical needs, and healthier people migrating to cheap out-of-state plans would weaken the risk pools they depend on.
